summary: Discusses models and design considerations for a SIP overload control mechanism. SIP servers can run out of resources and the 503 response code provides only limited protection, so overload remains a danger. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: SIP servers can become overloaded when they receive more messages than they can process. This RFC explains design choices for signaling overload and reducing traffic before retries make the problem worse.

questions: how to prevent sip server overload
subtitle: Design choices for controlling overload in networks of SIP servers.

tldr.problem: A Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) server can receive more messages than it can process. Retries after dropped or delayed messages can add still more load.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes a system model and compares explicit and implicit feedback, different server cooperation models, and several ways to limit traffic.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational design guide, not a protocol specification for one overload-control mechanism.

facts.label: Explicit feedback types
facts.value: Rate, loss, window, and signal based

today: RFC 6357 is an Informational document published in August 2011. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The SIP Overload Problem
sections.content:
SIP servers handle messages used to set up and manage communications. A server is overloaded when incoming messages exceed the resources it can use to process them. The existing 503 Service Unavailable response provides only limited overload control.

When a message is dropped or delayed, a sender may retransmit it. Those retries increase the load on a server that is already struggling, which can further reduce the number of messages it completes. The RFC discusses mechanisms intended to control this load.
sections.plainLanguage: A SIP server is overloaded when it cannot process all the messages it receives. Repeated attempts to resend messages can add to its workload.

sections.title: Parts of an Overload-Control System
sections.content:
The RFC's model has a SIP processor, a monitor, a control function, and an actuator. The monitor measures load and reports it to the control function. The control function decides whether to set a throttle and sends feedback to an upstream sender.

The actuator applies the throttle by controlling which messages are forwarded, rejected, or redirected. The details depend on the mechanism. A receiving server may have several upstream senders, so the design also needs to decide how it shares capacity among them.
sections.plainLanguage: A monitor measures a server's workload. A control function decides how much traffic to accept, and an actuator applies that limit.

sections.title: Who Cooperates and How Feedback Works
sections.content:
Hop-by-hop control uses a separate feedback loop between neighboring servers. It is comparatively simple, but feedback does not travel past the direct upstream neighbor. End-to-end control gathers overload information along a request path and can act farther upstream, but it must handle changing routes and more information.

Local control measures and rejects excess messages at the same server. It can provide a last layer of protection, but rejection itself uses resources. The RFC also distinguishes explicit feedback, which tells a sender to reduce traffic, from implicit feedback, where a sender infers overload from missing or delayed responses.
sections.plainLanguage: Neighboring servers can tell each other to reduce traffic, or a sender can infer a problem from missing responses. A server can also reject excess messages locally, but that alone may not prevent overload.

sections.title: Traffic Limits and Evaluation
sections.content:
Explicit feedback can specify a request rate, a percentage of messages to reject, a limit on unconfirmed messages, or an overload signal. These approaches make different demands on the servers. For example, rate-based control needs to account for upstream neighbors, while a window-based approach limits how many messages may be in transit without confirmation.

The RFC identifies goodput, delay, responsiveness, stability, fairness, and computational load as factors for evaluating a mechanism. It also notes that overload feedback creates security concerns: a malicious server could falsely claim overload, and upstream servers may fail to follow a requested reduction.
sections.plainLanguage: Servers can limit traffic in several ways, such as setting a rate or rejecting a share of messages. A design should also consider delay, fairness, security, and whether it remains stable as load changes.
